story_text.value:
Hi HN,

Have you ever been using Claude Code or Codex and run into a limit that ruined your flow? Claude says you’ve hit your limit but you’re knee deep in a refactor and want to keep going. Switching to Codex in that situation requires either having up-to-date handoff docs or rebuilding context from scratch. In both cases, you burn tokens just to handle moving context from one thread to another. Or maybe you have a great session, then compaction comes along and your agent forgets half of the important details.

I run into this a lot. Furthermore, I’m tired of one-off agents that can’t keep a stable identity across independent threads. I don’t want to be locked into Anthropic’s walled garden, or OpenAI’s ecosystem, I want to move freely as I see fit.

That’s why I built Crosshead. It’s more than a memory bank: it tracks the tasks, decisions and details that matter when work moves to a new thread. Your agent gets a stable cryptographic identity (a Nostr keypair) that carries across threads and tools, and handoffs are signed with it. Hooks inject context at each turn, so the agent always has the most important information available.

In my benchmarks of carrying task state into a new session, Crosshead passed 98% of fresh tasks, compared to 86% for claude-mem and 50% for Claude Code’s built-in memory. It also cost less per run than the other memory tools I tested, though built-in memory and a plain handoff file were a little cheaper. Details can be found here: https://crosshead.sh/benchmark

The catch is that it does not outperform when resuming the same session since caching is so cheap. Crosshead is best for people and agents who frequently encounter compactions, restarts, and harness/runtime switching. I am looking for folks interested in testing it with agents that are created and torn down frequently but need to retain context, like customer support or research agents.

It’s set up as a freemium service. Hot memory is free, and warm/cold memory is paid. I have added other features too, which are also paid via credits. You can purchase credits via Stripe or Lightning micropayments. The CLI and hooks are open source (https://github.com/FriendMachine/crosshead), and warm/cold memory and other features are hosted. Hot memory is synced first to a daemon on your machine then to the hosted service, so hot memory is also available offline. For other agents, there are native integrations for Hermes and OpenCode, an embeddable runtime for Pi agents, and an HTTP API. Show your agent https://crosshead.sh/skills/crosshead-bootstrap/SKILL.md to have it set itself up.

If you are interested in testing it, I recommend installing it in a single project first with

  curl -fsSL https://crosshead.sh/install | bash -s -- --add-to-path
  cd your-project
  crosshead quickstart --scope project --adapter both --api-base https://crosshead.sh --source-excerpts on
(The benchmark results depend on source excerpts, which is why the command turns them on. With them off Crosshead passed 50% of the main tasks. Excerpts are short pieces of the files and command output your agent reads. They sync to the hosted service in plaintext, not end-to-end encrypted, so leave the flag off if you are sensitive about sharing that.)

I am eager to hear your thoughts. I can imagine some of the pushback already, but you always surprise me with your critiques.

title.value: Show HN: Crosshead - Working memory and persistent identity for agents

story_text.value:
You pick your sections: news, crossword, chess, Kanji or D&D. Get one PDF on your Kindle every morning. If you have a stylus, you can write by hand and mail it back: your kanji get graded and your D&D move is read. The Kindle Scribe only accepts PDF by email and that channel is so simple that any e-reader (or plain inbox) works too.

I'm a developer of 30 years who's also a novelist. I wanted to see if I could build a SaaS with Claude Code. See https://ronanod.substack.com/p/the-music-of-code for my essay on the project.

The service is free and you can check out the AGPLv3 code: https://github.com/RonanOD/dailyscribe

What would you like on your device every morning?

story_text.value:
Hi everyone, I'm Ricardo and I've made a (free & Open Source) macOS app for knowing where my Claude Code subscription tokens went.

I think subscription allowance will either be limited in the near future or prices will go up, that's why I've started trying to optimise my prompts and tools.

Using Wake I've discovered interesting things like I can cut $0.50 in tokens to just $0.02 on large contexts if I clear the context just before asking the agent to commit the changes. In the latest version, I've also added a feature to understand what specific prompt caused a line change in my code.

At the moment, just macOS and Claude Code is supported, but I'm happy to add other OS or coding agents if there is interest.

If you have any feedback or question, I'm here to answer :)

Thanks for your time. Happy coding!

story_text.value:
Hi HN, my team just released box by Simular, a cloud computer for all your agents, with fast computer use built-in.

box gives your agents one remote Ubuntu desktop with Chrome and a shell, which your AI can then drive over MCP while your own computer stays unoccupied.

That means you can turn your basic ChatGPT plan into a personal agent by giving it a box computer; let your Claude Code pick up what Codex has left off on the same box to maximize usage; actually close your laptop and let tasks run in one persistent, 24/7 environment with all your logins and setup.

Some box demos: https://x.com/SimularAI/status/2121329778896871665?a=U4U1yYT...

We started on this because we believe computers shouldn't need human operation in the future. When agents arrived, people started running them on mini computers and you see colleagues walk around the office with their laptop lid open. We think there's a better solution - cloud computers engineered for agents.

Simular started three years ago to build out the full stack of an autonomous computer. box is our attempt to give agents a body to live in.

Our computer use outperformed Opus and GPT on OSWorld, costing fewer tokens. https://thenewstack.io/sai-agent-osworld-benchmark/

Copy/paste one command into your agent to start:

"Set up box from https://box.simular.ai/install"

You can watch box's live action from a dashboard https://box.simular.ai/box

We'd love for you to try it and share your feedback. I'll be in comments here to answer any question.

story_text.value:
View runs small rust programs as native interfaces using Rust and GPUI. Coding agents write and edit the programs. Changes load without restarting the app.

Each view has its own state and permissions. Views access data through APIs, CLIs or MCP servers.

It supports Pi, Codex, Claude Code and OpenCode and more. Saved state is encrypted locally. Credentials are stored in macOS Keychain.

story_text.value:
hi HN, I'm AJ.

Have been using Claude Code every day, and I was done re-typing the same project rules in every new chat. So I built this.

We try to follow some rules in our coding projects. For eg: "we use pnpm, not npm". The problem is, i tell claude about this rule in one chat, when i start another chat, i have to retype it. Also, when my team opens the same repo using another ai tool lets say cursor, they dont see the rule in their chat. Not cool.

So I built jevmem. It saves your project's rules in a file in your repo. and before Claude Code runs a command, it checks the command against those rules.

How it works:

1) You chat with Claude Code like normal.

2) jevmem saves your rules, decisions and everything that failed, one line each, in a file called JEVMEM.md in your repo.

3) You commit JEVMEM.md like any other file.

4) Claude Code, Cursor and Codex can all read it. now, your team also gets it when they pull.

for example: on Mon you tell Claude "we use pnpm, not npm". On Tuesday your teammate pulls and opens the repo in Cursor. They can see the pnpm rule.

oh and guard is my favourite part. So before Claude Code runs a command or edits a file, jevmem checks it against your rules. If it may break one of your rules, Claude Code stops and asks you first.

Eg: your rule is "don't hand-edit db/migrations/, those files are generated". 3weeks later, in a new session if claude tries to edit a migration, Claude Code stops and shows:

jevmem: this may break a saved rule: "Don't hand-edit db/migrations/: those files are generated." (JEVMEM.md)

You can also retrieve failed attempt. Like if you tried caching API responses in memory, and it broke the build, claude will remember that and some time later when you do the same thing, Claude tells you "Already tried: ..." with the reason.

Numbers from our tests:

-> Claude broke a project rule and left it in the code: 0 of 15 sessions with jevmem, 9 of 15 without it. We checked each one by hand.

-> Claude followed decisions made earlier in the project: 66 of 72 sessions with jevmem, 28 of 72 without.

Tbh, a CLAUDE.md file that you keep updating yourself did about as well here (67 of 72). The difference is that jevmem updates the file for you, likewise for cursor and codex.

jevmem also works alongside Claude Code's own auto memory. It doesn't replace it.

The catches:

- The guard works in Claude Code only. - You need a paid TypeSafe API key. jevmem's requests are billed to that key. - Your message text is sent to TypeSafe to be scored. Common secrets are removed first. - Nothing stored remotely. You turn it on per project. - We ran the tests on our own test projects.

(MIT license) Full results: https://avinash-jetwani.github.io/jevmem/results/

Install:

1. In claude: Plugins > Discover > jevmem > Add

2. npm install -g jevmem

3. In your project folder: jevmem setup

Repo: https://github.com/Avinash-jetwani/jevmem

I'd like to hear about your genuine feedback and how we could make it better!

title.value: Show HN: Jevmem – Auto Tracked Project Rules for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor
